title: Network troubleshooting with command-line tools
summary: Bring it all together with the command-line tools every technician relies on: ping, ipconfig, tracert, nslookup, and netstat, plus a repeatable troubleshooting method.
objectives: Use ping to test reachability and measure latency
Read ipconfig output to confirm a device's configuration
Use tracert to find where along a path traffic fails
Query DNS with nslookup to isolate name resolution faults
Apply a bottom-up, layered troubleshooting method
Combine tools to diagnose a realistic connectivity ticket

quiz.q: What does the ping command test?
options: Whether a host is reachable and the round-trip time
quiz.why: Ping sends ICMP echo requests and reports whether replies come back and how long the round trip takes, measuring reachability and latency.

options: Each router hop along the path to a destination
The MAC address of every device
quiz.why: Tracert lists each router hop and its response time, so you can see exactly where along the path traffic slows down or stops.

quiz.q: A ping to 8.8.8.8 succeeds but ping to google.com fails. What is the likely cause?
quiz.why: Reaching an IP but not a name means connectivity is fine and DNS is failing to resolve the name to an address.

quiz.q: Which command renews a device's DHCP lease on Windows?
quiz.why: ipconfig /renew requests a fresh IP configuration from the DHCP server, often paired with ipconfig /release beforehand.

quiz.q: Name the loopback address you ping to confirm the local TCP/IP stack works.
quiz.why: 127.0.0.1 (localhost) is the loopback address; a successful ping confirms the device's own TCP/IP stack is functioning before you test the network.

quiz.q: In one sentence, describe the bottom-up troubleshooting approach.
quiz.answer: Start at the physical layer and work up, checking the cable and link, then local IP config, then the gateway, then the internet, then DNS, until the failing layer is found.
quiz.why: Working methodically from Layer 1 upward isolates the fault to one layer instead of guessing, which is faster and more reliable.

body_markdown:
## Tools turn panic into method

When a user says "the internet is broken," a junior tech guesses and a good tech **tests**. A handful of command-line tools, used in a logical order, will diagnose almost every connectivity ticket you meet. This lesson brings the whole module together into a repeatable method.

## ping: is it reachable?

**ping** sends a small message and times the reply. It answers two questions: *can I reach this host?* and *how fast is the round trip?*

```bash
ping 8.8.8.8

Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=32 time=14ms TTL=118
Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=32 time=13ms TTL=118
```

Replies mean reachable; **Request timed out** or **Destination host unreachable** means a problem. Always ping a few targets in order: `127.0.0.1` (your own stack), your gateway, a public IP like `8.8.8.8`, then a name.

## ipconfig: what is my configuration?

**ipconfig** shows your address, mask, and gateway, and confirms whether DHCP worked. Use `/all` for DNS servers and MAC address, and `/release` `/renew` `/flushdns` to fix DHCP and DNS issues.

```bash
ipconfig /all
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /flushdns
```

A `169.254.x.x` address here tells you DHCP failed before you waste time elsewhere.

## tracert: where does it break?

**tracert** (traceroute) maps every **router hop** between you and a destination, with timing for each. It shows *where* along the path traffic slows or stops.

```bash
tracert example.com

  1    1 ms   192.168.1.1      (your router)
  2   12 ms   10.20.0.1        (your ISP)
  3    *    *    *   Request timed out
```

If the first hop fails, the problem is local; if it dies several hops out, the fault is upstream at the ISP — not something you can fix, but vital to know.

## nslookup: is DNS working?

**nslookup** queries DNS directly. If `ping 8.8.8.8` works but names fail, `nslookup` confirms the DNS fault and shows which server answered.

```bash
nslookup example.com
```

## A repeatable method

Work **bottom-up** through the layers and stop at the first failure:

```text
1. Physical: link light, cable seated?            (Layer 1)
2. ipconfig: valid IP, not 169.254.x.x?           (Layer 3 local)
3. ping gateway: can I reach my router?           (LAN)
4. ping 8.8.8.8: can I reach the internet by IP?  (routing/ISP)
5. nslookup / ping a name: does DNS resolve?      (Layer 7)
```

Each step that passes rules out a layer; the first that fails is your fault. This single checklist will solve the majority of your network tickets.

## Your task

Run the full bottom-up sequence on your own PC: `ping 127.0.0.1`, then ping your gateway, then `ping 8.8.8.8`, then `nslookup example.com`. Record the result of each. Then run `tracert 8.8.8.8` and count how many hops it takes to reach Google's DNS. Write a one-line conclusion stating that your connection is healthy at every layer.

Request timed out, or destination host unreachable, means a problem. The trick is to ping targets in order: one twenty-seven dot zero dot zero dot one, your own stack, then your gateway, then a public I P like eight dot eight dot eight dot eight, and finally a name.

ipconfig /all reveals DNS servers and MAC.
release, renew, flushdns fix DHCP and DNS.

slides.narration: Next, i p config. It shows your address, mask, and gateway, and confirms whether D H C P worked. Use slash all to also see your D N S servers and MAC address. And use slash release, slash renew, and slash flush d n s to fix D H C P and D N S issues. Remember: a one sixty-nine dot two fifty-four address here tells you D H C P failed, so you don't waste time looking elsewhere.

slides.title: tracert: where does it break?
bullets: Maps every router hop to a destination.
Shows timing for each hop along the path.
First hop fails: the problem is local.
Dies several hops out: the fault is upstream at the ISP.
slides.code:
tracert example.com
 1  1 ms  192.168.1.1
 2  12 ms 10.20.0.1

slides.narration: Now tracert, or traceroute. It maps every router hop between you and a destination, with timing for each one. This shows you where along the path traffic slows or stops. If the very first hop fails, the problem is local, on your machine or router. But if it dies several hops out, the fault is upstream at your provider. That's not something you can fix, but knowing it is vital, so you escalate instead of wasting hours.

slides.title: nslookup: is DNS working?
bullets: Queries DNS directly.
Confirms a DNS fault when names fail.
Shows which DNS server answered.
Works by IP but not name = DNS problem.
slides.narration: We've met this one already: n s lookup queries D N S directly. If pinging eight dot eight dot eight dot eight works but website names fail, n s lookup confirms the D N S fault and shows you which server answered. This is the tool that separates a name resolution problem from a true connectivity problem, and that distinction saves you enormous amounts of time.

slides.narration: Here's the method to memorise. Work bottom-up through the layers and stop at the first failure. One: check the physical link light and cable. Two: i p config for a valid address. Three: ping your gateway. Four: ping eight dot eight dot eight dot eight for the internet by I P. Five: n s lookup a name to test D N S. Each step that passes rules out a layer, and the first one that fails is your fault. This checklist alone solves most tickets.

slides.title: A worked ticket
bullets: User: my email won't load, internet is down.
ipconfig: valid IP, good. Ping gateway: replies.
Ping 8.8.8.8: replies. So the link is fine.
nslookup fails: it's DNS. flushdns and retry.
slides.narration: Let's work a real ticket. A user says their email won't load and the internet is down. You run i p config, the address is valid, good. You ping the gateway, it replies. You ping eight dot eight dot eight, it replies, so the link to the internet is fine. Then you run n s lookup and it fails. There's your answer: it's a D N S problem. You flush the D N S cache, retry, and email loads. Method, not guesswork, found it in under a minute.
